mcqs.question: Why is applying dependency inversion to config reads, via a ConfigProvider interface, valuable?
options: It makes config reads faster than a direct environment lookup
It lets application code depend on a stable abstraction instead of a specific source, so swapping env vars for a remote config service only touches the provider implementation, not every caller
It's required because environment variables can't be read from application code directly
It removes the need for any config values to have defaults
mcqs.explanation: Dependency inversion here means callers only know the ConfigProvider contract, so changing the underlying source is a one-place change, not a codebase-wide one. It's not about speed, environment variables are perfectly readable directly (that's the anti-pattern being avoided), and defaults are still very much needed.

mcqs.question: In LiveConfigProvider, why does reload replace the whole config snapshot atomically rather than mutating individual keys in place?
options: Because the language requires all maps to be immutable
Because mutating individual keys is faster than swapping the whole map
Swapping the whole snapshot atomically prevents a caller from reading one value from the old config and a related value from the new one mid-reload
Because a volatile field can only ever hold a Map object
mcqs.explanation: An atomic whole-snapshot swap avoids a torn read where different keys come from different points in time — a real risk if individual keys were mutated in place during a reload. There's no such immutable-map language requirement, per-key mutation isn't meaningfully faster here, and volatile isn't restricted to Map types.

mcqs.question: How does a component get notified when a specific config value changes, rather than just seeing the new value on its next get() call?
options: It polls get() in a tight loop until the value changes
It restarts the config provider on a timer
It reads the config file's last-modified timestamp directly
It subscribes to an optional change-listener hook the provider exposes alongside its plain get() method
mcqs.explanation: An explicit change-listener hook lets components react to a change event instead of only ever seeing the new value passively next time they call get(). Tight-loop polling, restarting the provider, or reading file timestamps directly are all workarounds that bypass the abstraction rather than use it.

mcqs.question: Why does caching a config value in a static field inside application code, instead of behind the ConfigProvider, break live reload?
options: The cache lives outside the provider's control, so it keeps returning the stale value forever even after the provider's underlying snapshot has changed
Static fields can't hold string values in most languages
It causes the ConfigProvider interface to no longer compile
It actually makes live reload work faster with no downside
mcqs.explanation: A cache outside the provider never sees a reload happen, so that one caller silently drifts from the current config indefinitely — exactly the bug live reload exists to prevent. Static fields hold strings fine, nothing here breaks compilation, and this is a real bug, not a performance win.
